newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss plan for humanitarian foundation gets boost.
newsitem.headline: Swiss plan for humanitarian foundation gets boost.

text.p: Switzerland's plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc ($4.9 billion) humanitarian fund by selling some official gold reserves got a shot in the arm on Thursday when cantonal finance chiefs endorsed the idea but with conditions.

The Conference of Cantonal Finance Directors (FKD) backed the plan at their annual meeting in Glarus after discussing their concerns with its leading champions at the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and federal finance ministry.
A statement said the conference "supports the government's intention to create the Solidarity Foundation in 1998 as testimony to Switzerland's humanitarian tradition."

The government needed support from the politically influential group to help to persuade voters to back the plan in a referendum next year that is shaping up as a watershed event in Swiss foreign relations and domestic politics.

The plan, announced by Swiss President Arnold Koller in March, calls for revaluing official gold reserves -- now on the SNB books at less than a third of their market value -- by 14 billion francs, half of which would finance the fund.

Gradually selling seven billion worth of gold and investing the proceeds in securities would generate around 350 million Swiss francs a year to distribue to victims of poverty, human rights abuses and disasters in Switzerland and abroad.

The fund would be separate from a 265 million Swiss franc Holocaust memorial fund that Swiss banks, other private businesses and the SNB are financing to alleviate the suffering of needy Holocaust survivors and their families.

Opinion polls taken immediately after the announcement showed most Swiss backed the idea of creating the humanitarian foundation, which the government hopes will clear the air of allegations that Switzerland cynically profited from World War Two.
But resistance to the idea has grown, fuelled by charges from right-wing politicians that Switzerland was being blackmailed from abroad into selling off national treasures.
Some cantonal officials have also grumbled that they should have been consulted before Koller made the announcement because cantons are large shareholders in the central bank.
While supporting the foundation in principle, they said its goals had to be clarified so that the fund did not compete against state or private social welfare programmes.

The cantons suggested that the SNB should manage all gold revaluation profits itself rather than hand them over to the foundation. "No doubts may be allowed to arise about currency stability," the directors said.

The cantons, as SNB shareholders, also want to protect their claims to SNB assets by insisting that the central bank must retain the second part of revaluation profits that are not used for the foundation.

At the end of last year, cantons, cantonal banks and other public authorities and institutions held 63 percent of the SNB's shares. Private shareholders had 37 percent, of which 70 percent were individials and 30 percent legal entities.
